description: How bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists cause communicable disease in humans and plants.
content_html:
Health and Disease

Health is a state of physical and mental well-being — not simply the absence of illness. Disease disrupts the normal functioning of cells and tissues, producing symptoms. Diseases fall into two broad categories: communicable diseases, which can be passed between organisms, and non-communicable diseases, which cannot. Understanding the causes and routes of spread of communicable diseases is essential for preventing and controlling them in both human and plant populations.

Key Fact

Communicable diseases are caused by pathogens — microorganisms that infect a host and cause harm. The four main types of pathogen are bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists. Each causes disease differently and requires a different approach to treatment or prevention.

The Four Types of Pathogen

Bacteria are single-celled prokaryotes. They can reproduce rapidly inside the body and cause disease in two main ways: by producing toxins (poisonous substances that damage host tissues) or by directly invading and destroying cells. Examples of human bacterial diseases include Salmonella food poisoning (transmitted through contaminated food or water) and Gonorrhoea (a bacterial sexually transmitted infection). Crown gall disease, caused by the bacterium Agrobacterium tumefaciens, affects plants by producing tumour-like growths on stems and roots.

Viruses are not cells — they are much smaller than bacteria and cannot reproduce outside a living host cell. Once inside, a virus injects its genetic material and hijacks the cell’s machinery to make thousands of new virus particles. The cell is often destroyed as new viruses burst out. Human viral diseases include influenza (spread by airborne droplets), HIV (spread through bodily fluids, causing AIDS), and in plants, tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) which causes distinctive mosaic patterning on leaves and reduces photosynthesis.

Fungi cause disease by growing on host tissue and releasing enzymes that break down cells. Athlete’s foot is a common human fungal infection affecting the skin between the toes. Ash dieback is a serious fungal disease that has devastated ash tree populations across Europe; the fungus prevents water flow through the tree, causing progressive dieback of branches and often death of the tree.

Protists are single-celled eukaryotes. The malaria parasite (Plasmodium) is a protist transmitted by the bite of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. Once inside the human body, the parasite infects and destroys red blood cells, causing the cycles of fever that characterise malaria. Mosquitoes act as vectors — they carry the parasite between human hosts without being harmed by it themselves.

How Pathogens Spread

Different pathogens use different routes to move between hosts. Understanding transmission routes is central to designing effective prevention strategies. Common routes include:

  • Airborne droplets: coughing or sneezing releases tiny droplets carrying pathogens. Influenza spreads this way.
  • Direct contact: touching an infected person or surface. Athlete’s foot spreads through contact with contaminated surfaces in warm, damp places.
  • Contaminated food or water: Salmonella is ingested in undercooked food or water contaminated with infected animal waste.
  • Bodily fluids: HIV is transmitted through blood, sexual contact, and from mother to child during birth or breastfeeding.
  • Animal vectors: malaria is transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes; the mosquito carries the parasite but does not develop the disease itself.
Key Fact

Plant diseases in this topic: tobacco mosaic virus (viral) — mosaic leaf patterns, reduced photosynthesis; ash dieback (fungal) — branch dieback and tree death; crown gall disease (bacterial) — tumour-like growths on stems and roots. All three can devastate populations of their host plant species.

The Body’s Natural Barriers

The human body has several non-specific defences that prevent pathogens from entering in the first place. These are described as non-specific because they act against any pathogen — they do not require the body to have encountered the pathogen before. The skin forms a physical barrier — unbroken skin is impermeable to most pathogens. In the respiratory tract, mucus traps pathogens and tiny hair-like structures called cilia sweep the mucus (with its trapped pathogens) away from the lungs. The stomach produces acid at a very low pH that kills most ingested pathogens. Tears and saliva contain enzymes (lysozyme) that break down bacterial cell walls. Beneficial bacteria in the gut occupy the available space and resources, competing with pathogens and making it harder for them to establish an infection.

If a pathogen does breach these first-line defences and enters the bloodstream or tissues, the immune system responds specifically to that pathogen. White blood cells called lymphocytes produce antibodies that bind to antigens on the pathogen’s surface, disabling or marking it for destruction. Other white blood cells can engulf and digest pathogens directly — a process called phagocytosis. Understanding these defences is essential for understanding how vaccines and other interventions work to enhance the body’s natural protection.

Plants have physical defences including a waxy leaf cuticle that prevents pathogen entry, and a cellulose cell wall that pathogens must breach to infect the cell. Plants also have chemical defences: they can produce antimicrobial substances in response to infection that slow or prevent pathogen spread within plant tissues. These active responses mean that the plant’s immune system, though simpler than a mammal’s, is dynamic — it responds to infection rather than simply acting as a passive barrier.
exam_tip_html: When answering questions about specific diseases, always state the type of pathogen (virus, bacterium, fungus or protist) and the route of transmission — two separate points that each earn marks. For plant diseases specifically, you are expected to recall tobacco mosaic virus, ash dieback and crown gall disease by name. If asked to ‘explain’ how a pathogen causes disease (not just ‘state’), include the mechanism: toxin production for bacteria, cell destruction for viruses, enzyme release for fungi, or cell invasion for protists.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Communicable diseases are caused by pathogens: bacteria (produce toxins or invade cells), viruses (hijack host cell machinery), fungi (release enzymes), and protists (invade and destroy cells). Each group has distinct examples in humans and plants.
  • Key named diseases: influenza and HIV (viral), Salmonella and crown gall (bacterial), Athlete’s foot and ash dieback (fungal), malaria (protist via mosquito vector), tobacco mosaic virus (viral, plant).
  • Pathogens spread via airborne droplets, direct contact, contaminated food/water, bodily fluids and animal vectors. The body’s non-specific defences (skin, mucus, stomach acid, lysozymes, gut bacteria) act as a first line of defence against all pathogens.

practice_questions.text: Name the type of pathogen that causes each of the following diseases: (a) influenza  (b) malaria  (c) athlete's foot  (d) tobacco mosaic virus in plants.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: all four correct — (a) virus, (b) protist, (c) fungus, (d) virus. Two marks for four correct. Secure: three correct. Developing: two correct. Emerging: one correct.

practice_questions.text: Describe how the malaria parasite is transmitted from one human host to another.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: the malaria parasite (Plasmodium, a protist) is carried by female Anopheles mosquitoes; the mosquito bites an infected person and takes up the parasite; the mosquito later bites another person, transferring the parasite into their bloodstream; the parasite infects red blood cells. Secure: mosquito as vector identified; transmission mechanism described; one step vague. Developing: states mosquito bites transmit malaria without identifying the parasite type or process. Emerging: vague reference to insects spreading disease.

practice_questions.text: Explain why viruses are more difficult to treat than bacterial infections.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: viruses reproduce inside host cells using the cell's own machinery; antibiotics target structures specific to bacteria (e.g. cell wall) but cannot kill viruses without damaging host cells; antiviral drugs exist but are harder to design because of this; the body's immune system must largely fight off viral infections. Secure: states viruses are inside cells and antibiotics don't work on viruses; mechanism of why partially explained. Developing: states antibiotics don't work on viruses but does not explain why. Emerging: states viruses are hard to treat without scientific reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Describe three non-specific defences that protect the human body against pathogens.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: any three from — skin (impermeable physical barrier); mucus and cilia in airways (traps and sweeps pathogens away from lungs); stomach acid (low pH kills ingested pathogens); tears/saliva lysozyme (enzyme breaks down bacterial cell walls); gut bacteria (compete with pathogens). Each defence described with its mechanism. Three defences with mechanisms = four marks. Secure: three defences named but one or two mechanisms missing. Developing: two defences with mechanisms. Emerging: one or two defences named without mechanisms.

practice_questions.text: A plant disease is spreading rapidly through a local woodland, causing trees to show leaf discolouration and reduced growth. A scientist suspects a fungal pathogen. Describe how the scientist could identify whether the pathogen is fungal, and explain one method to prevent further spread.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: describes taking a sample from an infected plant; culturing on agar; microscopy to identify fungal structures (hyphae, spores); or DNA analysis to confirm identity; notes that correct identification is essential before choosing a control strategy; prevention method: removing and destroying infected trees, preventing movement of infected material, chemical fungicide treatment, or biological control — with mechanism explained and reliability considered. Secure: identification method described adequately; prevention method with partial reasoning. Developing: mentions culture or microscopy but method is vague; prevention stated without explanation. Emerging: general reference to 'testing' without scientific method.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a communicable and a non-communicable disease, with one example of each.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: communicable = caused by a pathogen, can spread between organisms (e.g. influenza/Salmonella/HIV); non-communicable = not caused by an infection, cannot be passed on (e.g. type 2 diabetes/cancer/cardiovascular disease). Both defined with examples. Secure: both types defined correctly; one example missing. Developing: one type defined correctly. Emerging: vague distinction without reference to pathogens or examples.

flashcard_questions.a: A microorganism that causes disease in a host.

flashcard_questions.q: What type of pathogen causes influenza?

flashcard_questions.a: By producing toxins or directly invading and damaging host cells.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must viruses reproduce inside a host cell?
flashcard_questions.a: They cannot replicate independently — they need the host cell's machinery.

flashcard_questions.q: What pathogen type causes malaria, and how is it transmitted?
flashcard_questions.a: A protist (Plasmodium), transmitted by the bite of female Anopheles mosquitoes.

flashcard_questions.q: What plant disease does tobacco mosaic virus cause?
flashcard_questions.a: Mosaic patterning on leaves, reducing photosynthesis and stunting growth.

flashcard_questions.q: What type of pathogen causes ash dieback?
What type of pathogen causes crown gall disease in plants?

flashcard_questions.a: Through direct contact with contaminated surfaces in warm, damp environments.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the enzyme in tears and saliva that kills bacteria.
What is the role of cilia in the respiratory tract?
flashcard_questions.a: They sweep mucus (and trapped pathogens) away from the lungs.

flashcard_questions.q: What physical barrier do plants have on their leaves to resist pathogen entry?
What is a vector in disease transmission?
flashcard_questions.a: An organism that carries a pathogen between hosts without developing the disease itself.

glossary_terms.definition: Diseases caused by pathogens (bacteria, viruses, fungi or protists) that can be transmitted from one organism to another.
Single-celled prokaryotic microorganisms. Pathogenic bacteria cause disease by producing toxins or by directly damaging host cells.
Non-cellular pathogens that can only reproduce inside a living host cell. Viruses take over the cell's machinery to produce copies of themselves, often destroying the cell in the process.
A viral plant disease caused by tobacco mosaic virus that causes a mosaic of light and dark patches on leaves, reducing photosynthesis and stunting growth.
A fungal disease of ash trees caused by the fungus Hymenoscyphus fraxineus. It causes leaf wilting, bark lesions and progressive death of branches.
Eukaryotic organisms that include moulds and yeasts. Pathogenic fungi cause disease by growing on or inside a host and releasing enzymes that damage tissue.
Single-celled eukaryotic microorganisms that are neither plants, animals, nor fungi. Some protists are pathogenic parasites.
Molecules (usually proteins) on the surface of a pathogen that are recognised as foreign by the immune system and trigger an immune response.
A waxy, waterproof layer on the outer surface of a leaf that acts as a physical barrier against pathogens.
